en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on Food, 37.
The Training Rule on Eating at the Wrong Time.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time, there was a festival on the mountain peak in Rājagaha.
Seventeen groups of monks went to see the festival on the mountain peak.
When people saw the seventeen groups of monks, they had them bathe, anointed them, fed them, and gave them fresh foods to eat.
The group of seventeen monks, having taken fresh food and gone to the monastery, said this to the group of six monks:
“Friends, take some fresh food; eat! [They replied:
“Friends, from where did you obtain this fresh food?”
The group of seventeen bhikkhus informed the group of six bhikkhus of this matter:
“But why, friends, do you eat food at the wrong time?
“It is so, friends.”
The group-of-six monks grumbled, complained, and spread it about, saying:
“How can the group-of-seventeen monks eat food at the wrong time?
Then the group-of-six monks informed the monks of this matter.
Those bhikkhus who were of few desires... [and so on]... complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
"How can the group of seventeen bhikkhus eat food at the wrong time?"... [and so on]...
"Is it true, bhikkhus, that you eat food at the wrong time?"
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can you, foolish men, eat food at the wrong time? This is not for the benefit of non-believers…” [and so on].
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
‘Should any monk eat or consume solid or soft food at an improper time, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).’”
"But whoever" means whoever such a person... [as before] ...
"a bhikkhu."
... pe ... this is the meaning intended here by the term "bhikkhu.
"Improper time" (vikāla) means from when midday has passed until the rising of the dawn.
"Hard food" means the five kinds of cooked food;
excluding those things that are to be taken at the proper time, those to be taken for seven days, and those to be taken for life, the remainder is called "hard food.
"Soft food" means...
There are five kinds of food: boiled rice, sour gruel, flour, fish, and meat.
If one receives them with the intention, "I will chew it" or "I will eat it," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
For every swallow, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If, at an improper time, perceiving it to be an improper time, one eats or consumes solid or soft food, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If, at an improper time, being doubtful about it, one eats or consumes solid or soft food, there is an offense of expiation.
If, at an improper time, perceiving it to be a proper time, one eats or consumes solid or soft food, there is an offense of expiation.
If one accepts for the purpose of food that which is to be consumed within a watch of the day, within seven days, or for as long as life lasts, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
For every swallow, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is the proper time but one perceives it as the improper time, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is the right time, but he is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it is the right time and he perceives it as such, there is no offense.
There is no offense—
If he uses what is for a watch of the night, for seven days, or for as long as life lasts, when there is a suitable reason;
or if he is insane,
or if he is the first offender.
The seventh training rule concerning eating at the improper time is finished.
